title: Area with Fraction Side Lengths
short: Tile a rectangle with unit-fraction squares.

blocks.html: You know area = length × width for whole numbers, and you can multiply fractions. The formula still works when the sides are fractions, and tiling shows why.

The area of a rectangle with fraction side lengths is still length × width. Tiling it with small rectangles that are $\frac{1}{b}$ by $\frac{1}{d}$ gives the same answer: count the tiles and multiply by the area of one tile.

Cut a unit square into 4 columns and 3 rows. Each tile is $\frac{1}{4}$ by $\frac{1}{3}$, and 12 tiles fill the square, so each tile has area $\frac{1}{12}$. A rectangle $\frac{3}{4}$ long and $\frac{2}{3}$ wide holds 3 tiles across and 2 down: $3 \times 2 = 6$ tiles, an area of $\frac{6}{12}$. That is exactly $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{2}{3}$.

blocks.name: g5-fracarea
blocks.cap: A rectangle $\frac{3}{4}$ ft by $\frac{2}{3}$ ft, tiled inside a 1-foot square: 6 tiles of $\frac{1}{12}$ square foot.

blocks.title: Count the tiles
blocks.q: Find the area of a rectangle $\frac{3}{4}$ ft long and $\frac{2}{3}$ ft wide.
steps: Tiles $\frac{1}{4}$ by $\frac{1}{3}$ fit: 3 along the length and 2 along the width, so 6 tiles.
12 tiles make 1 square foot, so each is $\frac{1}{12}$ square foot.

blocks.title: Sides longer than 1
blocks.q: Find the area of a rectangle $\frac{5}{3}$ m by $\frac{3}{2}$ m.
steps: Tiling check: tiles $\frac{1}{3}$ by $\frac{1}{2}$ have area $\frac{1}{6}$, and 5 by 3 of them make 15.

blocks.name: g5-fracarea
blocks.cap: $\frac{5}{3}$ by $\frac{3}{2}$ spreads over more than one unit square: 15 tiles of $\frac{1}{6}$.

blocks.html: Forgetting that a tile is smaller than a unit square and calling the area “6 square feet” because there are 6 tiles. Check: the rectangle fits inside one square foot, so its area must be less than 1.
